## Backup correctness findings for Main

| System | Supported online method and concurrent-write behavior | WAL / recovery requirements and limits |
|---|---|---|
| **SQLite** | Use the [Online Backup API](https://www.sqlite.org/backup.html). SQLite says it holds the source lock only briefly while reading, allowing other users to continue; completed backup is a bitwise-identical snapshot from copy start. Writes during backup can restart copying, and external-connection writes are more expensive. | [WAL](https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html) permits readers with a writer, but **only one writer at a time**. WAL requires all processes on one host and does not work on network filesystems; it adds quasi-persistent `-wal` and `-shm` files. Long readers can prevent checkpoint progress, retaining/growing WAL. This is operational risk, not a claim about end-to-end backup reliability. |
| **PostgreSQL** | Use [continuous archiving/PITR](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/continuous-archiving.html) with a base backup, normally [pg_basebackup](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/app-pgbasebackup.html). The PITR documentation says files changing while an active base backup is copied are normal. This supports online operation, but the retained excerpts do **not** establish a stronger no-blocking/concurrent-writer guarantee. | Recovery requires a **continuous archived WAL sequence extending at least to the base-backup start**; configure and test WAL archiving before the first base backup. Restore replays WAL. A base backup cannot recover to a time during that backup; corrupt WAL halts recovery. WAL retention must cover the base-backup interval and recovery replay time. |

### Decisive official passages

- SQLite Backup API: “other database users [can] continue without excessive delays” and completion produces a “bit-wise identical copy … as it was when the copying commenced.” Writes mid-backup can cause restart, while the result remains a “consistent and up-to-date snapshot.”  
  https://www.sqlite.org/backup.html
- SQLite WAL: “writers and readers can run at the same time. However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time”; WAL requires same-host shared memory and “will not work on a network filesystem.”  
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- PostgreSQL PITR: recovery needs “a continuous sequence of archived WAL files that extends back at least as far as the start time of your backup”; `pg_basebackup` is the easiest base-backup method. Recovery target must be after base-backup end; corrupt WAL halts recovery.  
  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/continuous-archiving.html

### Applicability, contradictions, coverage

- **Version/date:** PostgreSQL links are the official `current` documentation, not version-pinned. SQLite WAL text explicitly notes read-only WAL opening behavior beginning in SQLite **3.22.0 (2018-01-22)**; other findings use the live official docs.
- **Contradictions:** None found. The SQLite reader/writer concurrency statement is not multiple-writer support.
- **Coverage:** Supported online method, SQLite writer/WAL constraints, and PostgreSQL WAL/PITR recovery prerequisites are covered. PostgreSQL’s exact write-blocking behavior during `pg_basebackup` remains a bounded documentation-excerpt gap.
- **Highest-impact resolving check:** inspect the exact `pg_basebackup` concurrent-client/locking passage for the deployed PostgreSQL major version.
